claims.text: Intense online communication with close friends was positively associated with mental well-being among 15-year-olds (b = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.57-2.70).
Intense online communication with larger friend groups was positively associated with mental well-being among 15-year-olds (b = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.44-1.62).
Moderate online communication with virtual friends was associated with poorer mental well-being among 15-year-olds (b = -1.02, 95% CI: -1.50, -0.43).
Intense online communication with virtual friends was associated with poorer mental well-being among 15-year-olds (b = -0.61, 95% CI: -1.14, -0.08).
The associations between online communication frequency across different friendship types and mental well-being remained robust after model adjustment.

evidence.description: Pooled cross-sectional linear regression showed that intense online communication with close friends had b = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.57-2.70 on the SWEMWBS scale.
Pooled cross-sectional linear regression showed that intense online communication with larger friend groups had b = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.44-1.62 on the SWEMWBS scale.
Moderate communication with virtual friends was linked to poorer well-being with b = -1.02, 95% CI: -1.50, -0.43.
Intense communication with virtual friends was linked to poorer well-being with b = -0.61, 95% CI: -1.14, -0.08.
The authors state that these associations remained robust even after model adjustment.

methodologies.name: Pooled cross-sectional linear regression modeling
methodologies.description: Examined associations between frequency of online communication with different types of friends and mental well-being measured by the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (SWEMWBS).
datasets: 2017/2018 Swedish Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) survey
2021/2022 Swedish Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) survey

limitations.text: Many previous studies have focused generally on time spent online rather than examining the specific nature of adolescents' online interactions.

future_work.text: Efforts to support young people's online activity should consider both the time spent online and the specific nature of their online interactions.
